blocks.text: Pretty in pink: the best of PhotoMonth 2026 – in pictures
This year’s London photography festival takes you from the colourful streets of Kolkata to the grim isolation units of Guantánamo Bay

blocks.alt: Kevin You, Encounters 2026, from Open Call, ‘Unity and Community’ Arts PavillionPhotoMonth 2026 is a month-long festival of photography exhibitions and events across artist-run spaces, independent galleries and major cultural institutions in London. The programme features a symposium, exhibition tours and an open call, Unity and Community.

blocks.text: Kevin You, Encounters 2026, Open Call, Unity and Community
PhotoMonth 26 is at various locations in London until 30 October 2026

links.text: PhotoMonth 26 is at various locations in London until 30 October 2026

blocks.alt: Megan Taylor, Siham, from The School Mothers Project, Open Call, ‘Unity and Community’ Arts PavillionBy including exhibitions by independent photographers and galleries, from across London, the event brings together longstanding members of London’s photography community and young breakthrough artists and thinkers who are actively shaping the future of the city’s art scene.

blocks.text: Megan Taylor, Siham, from The School Mothers Project, Open Call, Unity and Community

blocks.alt: Barry Lewis, from Blackpool in the 80sBarry Lewis: ‘As a kid from London, Blackpool seemed so far away in the north that it became an exotic chimera when I saw it on TV: miles of sandy beaches with donkey rides, not one but three piers, a huge fun-fair, a mile-long promenade full of fortune-tellers, pubs, fish-and-chip shops, plus the famous Illuminations along Promenade. It seemed the epitome of the British at play, with everyone’s guard down and pleasure ruthlessly pursued’

blocks.text: Barry Lewis, from Blackpool in the 80s

blocks.alt: Seamus Murphy, Para (পাড়া) Kolkata, 2026 In a city that’s constantly coming apart, breaking away, and remaking itself, Seamus Murphy’s camera uncovers a calm, deeply moving formalism. Vertical lines, borders, gaps between things: all these fascinate Murphy, as do the punctuations of everyday life (animals, human figures, machines, the remnants of a habitation) they contain

Lou Melchior, Green Mesh, from ‘The Van, the Sock and the Shadows’ In this solo exhibition, Melchior captures the incidental overlooked object, the passing shadow and the fragment of everyday life, and quietly turns them against themselves revealing a world at once intimate elusive and faintly absurd. The work invites us to reconsider what we believe we recognise and to consider the strange solitude that lies within our shared experience. Showing at Gallery 46
